extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical/philosophical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and qualities for judging works about ideal states and related philosophical dialogues (e.g., Plato, More, Bacon, Campanella): style, credibility, originality, use of sources, moral/political insight, and unity/coherence. Useful for literary or philosophical appraisal of utopian and Platonic-influenced writings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The comparatively short work called the Statesman or Politicus in its style and manner is more akin to the Laws, while in its idealism it rather resembles the Republic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a work’s tone and formal style to other canonical works; assess whether style is appropriate to its philosophical aims and how it relates (closer to law‑like practical prose or to idealistic dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between politics and dialectic / method
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In both the Republic and Statesman a close connection is maintained between Politics and Dialectic. In the Statesman, enquiries into the principles of Method are interspersed with discussions about Politics.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the work integrates methodological (dialectical) inquiry with political argument; examine whether methodological sections illuminate or disrupt political content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative influence and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of other writers note when they ‘approach’ Plato, ‘rival’ him, or merely ‘translate’ his portraits; e.g., Cicero ‘converts into a stately sentence the humorous fancy’ of Plato but is ‘far inferior’ in describing the tyrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge originality vs. borrowing: does the work add new insight or simply imitate canonical passages? Look for successful adaptation versus mere translation or clumsy imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and appropriateness of language (rhetoric vs dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero’s ‘manners are clumsy and inferior; the hand of the rhetorician is apparent at every turn’ and he is ‘making speeches, and is never able to mould the intractable Latin to the grace and ease of the Greek Platonic dialogue.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether rhetorical flourishes help or hinder philosophical discussion; assess linguistic grace, naturalness of dialogue, and suitability of prose to philosophical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The greater merit of the work is not the admirable art, but the originality of thought.’ (on More’s Utopia)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value new or unusually tolerant/perspective-shifting ideas over mere formal skill; consider how radical or anticipatory the political/moral proposals are for their time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility / verisimilitude of fictional framing
rubrics_metrics.description: More is praised for being ‘very precise about dates and facts, and has the power of making us believe that the narrator of the tale must have been an eyewitness.’ By contrast Bacon’s New Atlantis ‘by no means impresses the reader with a sense of credibility.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative devices used to create believability (precise detail, eyewitness framing); judge whether mixing of fact and fiction is persuasive or undermines the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic invention and art of feigning
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He is gifted with far greater dramatic invention than any one who succeeded him... In the art of feigning he is a worthy disciple of Plato.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imaginative skill in creating convincing fictions, narrators, and scenarios; consider how well dramatic invention serves the philosophical/political message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and handling of sources (critical vs uncritical)
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Augustine’s work ‘is wholly uncritical’ in use of Greek, Roman, and sacred writings; Dante’s arguments rely on ‘perversions of Scripture and history, by false analogies… and odd scraps and commonplaces of logic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author uses authorities and scriptures critically and appropriately or leans on misapplied quotations and weak analogies; assess scholarly rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument quality and logical soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dante’s necessity for an Universal Empire is proved ‘partly by a priori arguments… partly by perversions of Scripture and history, by false analogies… and by odd scraps and commonplaces of logic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate strength and method of argumentation: reliance on a priori reasoning, evidence, or fallacious uses of history/scripture; identify weak analogies and unsupported generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone toward religion and tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: More’s Utopia shows tolerance: ‘no prayers be used, but such as every man may boldly pronounce without giving offence…’ and they ‘put him to no punishment’ for disbelief though exclude him from administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the work treats religious diversity and dissent—whether it displays tolerance, coerces belief, or uses religion polemically; consider social implications of religious policy in the fictional state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical effectiveness and moral/political critique
rubrics_metrics.description: More is ‘full of satirical reflections on governments and princes’ and ridicules contemporary institutions (e.g., the new logic, sports of the gentry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how well satire exposes real-world vices and motivates reflection; consider subtlety, targets, and whether satire weakens or strengthens the work’s proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and reform proposals (social policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: More proposes concrete reforms: limiting labour to six hours, dislike of capital punishment, reformation of offenders, assigning idle people to useful occupations, sanitary reforms, and proposals about property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the feasibility and social reasoning of proposed policies; determine whether proposals are utopian fantasy, prudential reform, or prophetic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence of style/content
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon ‘has injured the unity of style by adding thoughts and passages which are taken from the Hebrew Scriptures.’ Campanella is ‘full of inconsistencies.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work maintains a consistent tone, integrates borrowed material organically, and avoids internal contradictions that weaken its persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of acquaintance with source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Campanella ‘shows but a superficial acquaintance with [Plato’s] writings’ and Augustine is ‘very slightly acquainted’ with Plato although ‘attracted’ to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the author’s actual understanding of the philosophical tradition they invoke; superficial borrowing is a weakness, deep engagement strengthens authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational theory and emphasis on natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Campanella ‘looks forward to a new mode of education, which is to be a study of nature, and not of Aristotle… He insists strongly on the necessity of a variety of knowledge.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work’s prescriptions for education: emphasis on empirical/natural study, breadth of curriculum, pedagogical methods (e.g., pictures vs books), and expected societal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of family, property, and gender roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions include communal wives/children, collective property, women trained in warlike exercises but with some special occupations, and state care of infants; More’s Utopia rejects private gold/silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the work handles private vs. communal property, family structures, and gendered division of labor—both ethical implications and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between ideal and practicable (distance vs approachability)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Ideals... are partly framed by the omission of particulars; they require to be viewed at a certain distance, and are apt to fade away if we attempt to approach them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the ideal is presented as a useful guiding vision or an impractical scheme; consider how omission of particulars functions rhetorically and whether more detail would help or harm the ideal’s credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/philosophical depth versus rhetorical ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The abstractions of philosophy are to most persons cold and vacant; they give light without warmth… Men cannot live by thought alone; the world of sense is always breaking in upon them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the balance between high abstraction and concrete human concerns; judge whether the work connects ideals to lived experience and moral feeling rather than mere verbal subtlety.
